How Well Do You Really Know Carbon-Phosphorus Double Bonds?
In studying organic chemistry, we seem to restrict our understanding of the reactivity of carbon-phosphorus double bonds to their “metathesis” reactions with carbon-oxygen double bonds. With the assistance of transition metals, however, double bonds between carbon and trivalent phosphorus display distinctive modes of formation and reactivity. In this problem, whenever a subquestion asks for the SMILES of a complex, supplement it with a verbal description of the specific coordination mode.

subquestions.text_open: 9-1 Carbon-phosphorus double bonds can be constructed in many ways and can coordinate to transition metals in more than one mode. 9-1-1 In the reaction below, [Mn] denotes (η^{5}-C_{5}H_{4}CH_{3})Mn(CO)_{2}, and the reaction produces 4 molecules of THF. Given that the major product contains 2 phosphorus-oxygen single bonds, write the SMILES structure of the major product. 4 [Mn]·THF + 2 ^{t}BuCP + H_{2}O →

9-1-2 The following example provides an initial illustration of the role played by transition metals in forming carbon-phosphorus double bonds. Use SMILES structures and any necessary verbal descriptions to represent the three key electrically neutral intermediates in the reaction. Coordination of double bonds to Mo need not be shown in any of them.

text_images.description: The reaction in the figure shows the anionic dinuclear molybdenum complex 'O=C[Mo](C=O)[Mo](PC1=CC=CC=C1)(C=O)C=O' reacting with acryloyl chloride, 'ClC(C=C)=O', to form a product in which the phosphaalkene ligand 'C/C=P\C2=CC=CC=C2' is bound to the dinuclear molybdenum framework 'O=C[Mo](C=O)[Mo](C=O)C=O'. In the reactant, a phenylphosphido group bridges two Mo atoms, each bearing two carbonyl ligands; on one side, a coordinate bond shown by an arrow points to the left Mo atom. After reaction, the newly formed phosphaalkene ligand coordinates in a bidentate bridging mode: the lone pair on phosphorus forms a coordinate bond, shown by an arrow, to the left Mo atom, while the $P=C$ double bond coordinates through a $\pi$ bond, shown by an arrow, to the right Mo atom.

text_images.description: Description of the structures/reaction in the figure: '[H]C#CC1=CC=CC=C1' undergoes steps involving NEt_3/PCl_3, ArLi, tBuLi, ML_n, and irradiation/O_2 to form a species whose ligand has the SMILES 'O=C(C(/C(C(C1=CC=CC=C1)=O)=P/C)=P\C)C2=CC=CC=C2'. The ligand coordinates to [ML_n] through its two P atoms. Ar denotes an aryl substituent, and [ML_n] denotes a metal coordination fragment.

subquestions.text_open: 9-2 An important class of reactions of carbon-phosphorus double bonds involves metal carbenes. 9-2-1 In the following reaction, addition between the two substrates gives A_{1}, and A_{1} then converts into its isomer A_{2}. A_{2} undergoes a hydrogen migration to give A_{3}; A_{3} eliminates HNMe_{2} to give A_{4}; and a further elimination gives A_{5} together with byproduct A_{6}. A_{5} undergoes a simple reaction to afford the final product. W remains six-coordinate throughout the process. In A_{2}, W is coordinated by the carbon-phosphorus double bond, whereas in A_{3}, A_{4}, and A_{6}, W is coordinated by P. On this basis, write the SMILES structures of A_{1}~A_{6}.

text_images.description: Description of the structures/reaction in the figure: 'CN(C)C(=P)N(C)C' reacts with 'C1CC1C(O[Si](C)(C)C)=[W]([C]#O)([C]#O)([C]#O)([C]#O)[C]#O' to form 'O=C1C2(CC2)C(=O)C13CC3'.

subquestions.text_open: 9-2-2 When the phosphorus atom no longer bears a hydrogen atom, a hydrogen migration analogous to the process above cannot occur. In the following reaction, the two substrates undergo a process similar to that in the preceding subquestion, proceeding through B_{1} to B_{2}. Write the SMILES structure of one key electrically neutral intermediate in the conversion of B_{2} to the products.

text_images.description: Description of the structures/reaction in the figure: 'CN(C)C(=P[Fe])N(C)C' + 'CCOC(=[M])C' -> 'CN(C)/C=C/C(=[M])OCC' + 'CCOC(C)=P([Fe])[M]. Here M denotes a metal. The ligands on Fe and M are omitted in this question.'
